passage: Beta, I am Manjula, and at twenty-four I had two offers, one to stay in Mysuru and one in Pune. My whole family had opinions. One uncle said government jobs only. An aunt said marry first, then travel. My cousin Arnab said Pune, hands down. Each opinion came with its own fear. I sat with my tea and listened without arguing, and wrote each worry in a small notebook. Then Arnab asked, "But what do you want?" I said I wanted to see Pune. I thanked everyone at dinner and told them my answer would come by Sunday. They were quiet, but nobody argued after that.

qa.q: What two offers did Manjula have at twenty-four?
qa.a: Manjula had two offers, one to stay in Mysuru and one in Pune.

qa.q: What might Manjula have been feeling while listening to each relative?
qa.a: Manjula was probably pressured and a little anxious, but stayed courteous, listening and writing each worry down instead of arguing.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Manjula's story?
qa.a: Arnab asked what Manjula wanted, and Manjula said Pune and told the family the answer would come by Sunday.

qa.q: What might Arnab have been thinking when asking "But what do you want?"
qa.a: Arnab probably saw that the others were giving advice from their own fears and wanted Manjula's wishes to be heard.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling conflicting, confident family advice and listening respectfully without handing over the decision.

passage: The Pune offer expired at nine the next morning, and tonight the whole family had come to dinner, with a pressure cooker whistling and a broken fan clicking over the noise. Uncle told Indu to stay in Hyderabad, where it was safe. Her mother said the pay was too low. Nandini, her cousin, said take it, or she'd regret it for years. Everyone spoke at once and no one asked her a question. Indu smiled and passed the dal. "Thank you all. I hear each of you." Afterwards she took her plate to the balcony, wrote what each person feared, and then what she wanted. At eight she decided.

qa.q: When did the Pune offer expire?
qa.a: The Pune offer expired at nine the next morning.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling as everyone spoke at once and no one asked her a question?
qa.a: Indu felt crowded and unheard, but she stayed polite, smiling and passing the dal.

qa.q: What did Indu do after dinner that helped her decide?
qa.a: She went to the balcony and wrote what each person feared and then what she wanted, before deciding.

qa.q: Why might Nandini urge Indu to take the offer?
qa.a: Nandini fears Indu will regret missing the chance for years, so the advice comes from Nandini's own worry about regret.

grounding: Shows a person deciding on a move while relatives give confident, conflicting advice and listening respectfully without giving up the decision.

passage: I'm Jahnavi, and when I got a job offer in Hyderabad, my whole family had an opinion. Nani said a girl shouldn't live alone in a big city. Chacha said the private sector was unstable and I should sit for government exams. My mother worried about the food. My cousin Ayesha, the only one who lived in Hyderabad, said, "Come! It's great." Each spoke with total confidence, and each was really talking about their own fears. I listened to all of them, thanked them, and felt pulled in four directions. Then I made a list of what I wanted, not what they feared. I took the job. Nani still sends me pickle every month.

qa.q: What did Chacha suggest instead of the job?
qa.a: Chacha said Jahnavi should sit for government exams.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel listening to all the advice?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt pulled in four directions by confident, conflicting opinions.

qa.q: What helped Jahnavi decide while still respecting the family?
qa.a: Listening and thanking everyone, then listing personal wants rather than the family's fears, kept the decision in Jahnavi's hands.

qa.q: How might Nani feel about Jahnavi's choice?
qa.a: Nani may still feel worried, but her monthly pickle suggests love and acceptance of the decision.

grounding: A young adult describes relatives giving confident, conflicting advice based on their fears, and listening without handing over the decision.

passage:
Career counsellor's note, Thursday.
Reena, twenty-five, came in today visibly tired. She has an offer to move to Singapore for work. She described a family meeting last weekend: her father fears she will not return, her aunt Nirmala insists that moving abroad is the only way to grow, and her grandmother fears for her marriage prospects. Each spoke firmly. Reena said, "I respect all of them. But it's like they're deciding their own lives through me." I suggested she write down her own reasons first, then share them with each relative separately, listening to their fears without agreeing to decide by them. She plans to talk to her father on Sunday. We meet again next week.

qa.q: Where has Reena been offered work?
qa.a: In Singapore.

qa.q: How was Reena feeling when she came in?
qa.a: She was visibly tired and felt pressured, as if relatives were deciding their own lives through her.

qa.q: What did the counsellor suggest, and why is it a good approach?
qa.a: Write her own reasons first, then talk to each relative separately, listening to their fears without handing over the decision.

qa.q: How might Reena's aunt Nirmala see the move?
qa.a: Nirmala sees it as the only way to grow, speaking from her own hopes and certainty rather than Reena's needs.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young woman facing confident, conflicting family advice and learning to listen without handing over the decision.

passage:
Dear Diary, Sunday
Told the family I'm thinking of leaving the bank job to become a physiotherapist. Mummy (Sudha) went pale and said I'd be throwing away security. Mama said physiotherapy doesn't pay. Chachi said I should first get married. My cousin said follow my passion. Everyone was so sure.
I didn't argue. I just listened, and wrote down each worry. Some were useful: money, how long the course takes. Some were just their fears.
I'm not deciding tonight. I'll speak to two physiotherapists this week and check the course fees. It's my life, and I still love them for caring. 🤍
Ojas

qa.q: What job does Ojas want to leave?
qa.a: The bank job.

qa.q: How does Ojas feel after the family discussion?
qa.a: Ojas feels pressured by everyone's certainty but calm and loving, choosing to listen without handing over the decision.

qa.q: What steps does Ojas plan, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Speaking to two physiotherapists and checking course fees, which tests the useful worries without being ruled by fear.

qa.q: How might Sudha feel about Ojas's plan?
qa.a: Sudha, who went pale, may feel frightened about lost security, speaking from her own fears as a mother.

grounding: A diary shows a young adult listening to confident, conflicting family advice while keeping the decision.

passage:
[Family group]
Mummy: Francis, ship job means eight months at sea. What if something happens? 😟
Uncle Joe: Hotel job is steady. Ships come and go. My friend's son came back with nothing.
Aunty Rita: Nonsense, go! Stay in Goa forever and you'll never see the world.
Mummy: Rita, don't encourage him.
Francis: Thank you all, really. I'm listening to every point. I'll decide by Sunday and tell you why.
[Private chat]
Binita: very diplomatic message 😅 you ok?
Francis: honestly my head is spinning. they're all so sure and all saying opposite things
Binita: they're sure about their own fears, not about your life
Francis: mummy's fear is the sea. uncle's is money. aunty's is being stuck
Francis: none of those is exactly mine
Binita: so what's yours?
Francis: missing too many years of home. I'll ask the cruise line about a shorter first contract
Binita: see, that's your own question 👍

qa.q: How long did Mummy say the ship job would keep Francis at sea?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: How is Francis feeling after the family group messages?
qa.a: He is overwhelmed and confused, with his head spinning, because everyone is so sure and says opposite things.

qa.q: What did Francis do well in his reply to the family?
qa.a: He thanked everyone and said he was listening, but kept the decision his own by promising to decide by Sunday and explain why.

qa.q: How does Mummy see the ship job?
qa.a: Mummy sees it through fear for his safety at sea, which is why she worries about what might happen and tells Rita not to encourage him.

grounding: Shows a young man whose relatives each give confident, conflicting career advice from their own fears, and who listens respectfully without handing over the choice.
